---
title: "Exercise: few labels"
---

## Goal

By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

- read a learning curve and estimate what more labels would buy *(math: fit a power law)*,
- plan sparse annotation and say what the loss does with unmarked pixels,
- run the human-in-the-loop cycle and an active-learning loop, and say when uncertainty sampling fails,
- keep the test set honest in an annotation campaign.

The questions under **By hand** and **Explore** are for everyone. The **Math questions** are for students who want the full treatment.

## Background

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Learning curve | accuracy or error against the number of labelled examples |
| Sparse annotation | a few objects outlined completely plus some background strokes; the rest unmarked |
| Human in the loop | predict, let a person correct, retrain, repeat |
| Active learning | the model proposes which examples to label next |
| Uncertainty | how close a prediction is to a toss-up; two classes: $1 - \lvert 2p - 1\rvert$ |
| Most different | the unlabelled example farthest from every labelled one |

## By hand

**B1.** A learning curve. Error rates of a network trained from scratch on 6, 30 and 300 labels: 38 %, 18 % and 3 %.
(a) Plot $\log(\text{error})$ against $\log N$ roughly. Is it close to a line?
(b) From 30 to 300 labels the error fell from 18 % to 3 %. If the slope stays, what error would 3000 labels give?
(c) A frozen probe reaches 2.7 % with 15 labels and stays there up to 300. What limits it, and what would help?

**B2.** Sparse annotation. An image of 400 × 400 pixels has 60 nuclei of about 300 pixels each. You outline 6 nuclei and paint background strokes covering 2000 pixels.
(a) How many pixels enter the loss, and what fraction of the image is that?
(b) How many nucleus pixels and background pixels are marked? Suggest class weights that make both classes count equally.
(c) What goes wrong if the 54 unmarked nuclei are counted as background?

**B3.** Uncertainty. Five unlabelled cells have $p(\text{class B}) = 0.9, 0.45, 0.6, 0.55, 0.02$.
(a) Compute $1 - \lvert 2p - 1\rvert$ for each. Which is labelled next by "most uncertain"? (Ties to the first.)
(b) The fifth cell is in fact class B. Will "most uncertain" ever pick it soon? What does that say about the 0.02?

**B4.** Most different. Labelled cells at $(0, 0)$ and $(1, 1)$; unlabelled at $(0.1, 0)$, $(0.5, 0.5)$, $(0, 0.9)$. Which is farthest from its nearest labelled cell?

**B5.** Results of the demo's rules (mean of 6 starts; test accuracy, and in brackets the fraction of rare cells correct):

| labels | 10 | 20 | 40 |
|---|---|---|---|
| random | 80.3 % (31) | 85.4 % (50) | 91.5 % (73) |
| most uncertain | 83.9 % (0) | 88.3 % (0) | 91.3 % (0) |
| uncertain + different | 81.7 % (49) | 92.8 % (71) | 94.3 % (74) |
| the model's mistakes | 80.5 % (70) | 90.8 % (78) | 96.5 % (87) |

(a) Which rule is best with 10 labels, and which with 40?
(b) Why does "most uncertain" end where random ends, although it led at 10 and 20?
(c) "The model's mistakes" needs something the others do not. What?

**B6.** A colleague picks the test cells with the same active-learning rule that picked the training cells, "to test on the interesting cells". Give two reasons why the reported accuracy would mislead.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions"}
**B1.** (a) $\log_{10}N$ = 0.78, 1.48, 2.48 and $\log_{10}$ error = −0.42, −0.74, −1.52: slopes $-0.32/0.70 = -0.46$ and $-0.78/1.0 = -0.78$; roughly a line, steepening (real curves bend). (b) One decade divided the error by 6, so another decade gives about $3/6 = 0.5$ %, if nothing flattens it. (c) Its fixed features: the probe cannot do better than the features allow (a floor). Tuning the backbone, or better features, not more labels.

**B2.** (a) $6 \cdot 300 + 2000 = 3800$ of $160{,}000$ pixels: 2.4 %. (b) 1800 nucleus and 2000 background pixels: almost balanced; weights $w \propto 1/\text{count}$, e.g. $1/1800$ and $1/2000$ (normalised: 1.05 and 0.95). (c) 16,200 nucleus pixels would be labelled background: the network learns to call nuclei background, and misses them.

**B3.** (a) 0.2, 0.9, 0.8, 0.9, 0.04. The second cell (0.45) is picked (tie with 0.55, which comes later). (b) No: with uncertainty 0.04 it is near the end of the queue. The model is confidently wrong; uncertainty sampling cannot see such mistakes.

**B4.** Distances to the nearest labelled cell: $(0.1, 0)$: 0.1; $(0.5, 0.5)$: 0.71; $(0, 0.9)$: $\min(0.9, \sqrt{1 + 0.01}) = 0.9$. The third, $(0, 0.9)$.

**B5.** (a) With 10: most uncertain (83.9 %); with 40: the model's mistakes (96.5 %), then uncertain + different (94.3 %). (b) It keeps labelling the boundary between the two big classes, which is learnt after about 20 labels, and never finds the rare subtype (0 % correct): the remaining errors are exactly the cells it never asks about. (c) A person must look at the predictions for every cell and know the true class to spot the mistakes: the human in the loop.

**B6.** The test cells are not a random sample of the cells you will analyse: hard, unusual cells are over-represented, so the accuracy is not the accuracy on your images (here probably too low; in general it is simply not interpretable). And they were chosen with the help of the model being tested: the choice depends on the training set and the model, so the test set is not independent of them (the [leakage unit](../leakage/lec.qmd)).
:::

### Math questions

**B7.** *(math)* Fit $\text{error} = aN^{-b}$ to two points $(N_1, e_1)$, $(N_2, e_2)$: give $b$ and $a$. Apply it to $(30, 0.18)$ and $(300, 0.03)$. How many labels does halving the error then need?

**B8.** *(math)* For two classes, show that the margin $1 - \lvert 2p - 1\rvert$, the entropy $H(p)$ and the least confidence $1 - \max(p, 1 - p)$ are all decreasing functions of $\lvert p - 0.5\rvert$, so they pick the same cell.

**B9.** *(math)* The sparse loss is $\mathcal L = \sum_i m_i\ell_i / \sum_i m_i$. Show that the gradient with respect to the network output at an unmarked pixel is 0. What is the gradient at a marked pixel?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions (math)"}
**B7.** *(math)* $b = \log(e_1/e_2)/\log(N_2/N_1)$, $a = e_1N_1^b$. Here $b = \log 6/\log 10 = 0.778$, $a = 0.18 \cdot 30^{0.778} = 2.53$. Halving needs $2^{1/b} = 2^{1.29} = 2.4$ times as many labels.

**B8.** *(math)* Let $t = \lvert p - 0.5\rvert \in [0, 0.5]$. Margin: $1 - 2t$. Least confidence: $1 - (0.5 + t) = 0.5 - t$. Entropy: $H(0.5 + t) = H(0.5 - t)$ is symmetric about 0.5 and strictly concave, so it decreases in $t$. All three are strictly decreasing in $t$: the cell with the smallest $t$ maximises all three.

**B9.** *(math)* $\partial\mathcal L/\partial\hat y_i = m_i\,\ell'(\hat y_i, y_i)/\sum_j m_j$, which is 0 when $m_i = 0$; at a marked pixel it is the usual per-pixel gradient divided by the number of marked pixels.
:::

## Explore: which cell next? {#explore}

A pool of 500 unlabelled cells, each described by two features. Two classes (blue A and orange B), and a small **rare subtype** of class B in the top-left corner (30 cells). The classifier (logistic regression on smooth bumps) starts from 4 labelled cells and is retrained after every new label; the background shows its $p(\text{B})$ and the black line its boundary. Choose the rule for the next label: **random**, **most uncertain**, **most different** (farthest from all labels), **uncertain + different** (in turn), or **the model's mistakes** (a person who sees all predictions labels a cell the model gets wrong). The red ring shows the proposed cell; **label 1** or **label 10** accepts proposals; clicking a cell labels it yourself. Right: test accuracy on 600 other cells; the lines are the mean of 6 runs from different starts, the dots this run.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../demos/dist/demo.css">
<div data-demo="activelearn" data-preset="uncertain"></div>
<script src="../demos/dist/activelearn.js"></script>
```

**E1.** Presets **random** and **most uncertain** (20 labels each). Compare where the labelled cells lie, and the test accuracy.

**E2.** Preset **uncertain misses the rare cells** (40 labels, true classes shown). How many rare cells were labelled? How is the rare subtype predicted, and why does uncertainty sampling never ask about it?

**E3.** Preset **uncertain + different** (40 labels). Where do the "different" labels go? Compare accuracy and rare cells with E2.

**E4.** Preset **a person fixes mistakes** (20 labels). Compare with the curves of the other rules at 20 labels. What is the catch?

**E5.** Start again and label cells yourself by clicking: try to beat 92 % with 15 labels. Which cells did you choose?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions"}
**E1.** Random: labels spread over the whole pool, 82.7 % after 20 labels. Most uncertain: labels crowd along the boundary between the moons, where they move it most: 88.2 %. (From this start; the mean curves: 85.4 and 88.3 %.)

**E2.** None of the 40 labelled cells is rare. The rare subtype sits deep in the region the model calls A, with $p(\text{B})$ near 0: the model is sure, and wrong, so the rare cells are never uncertain. Test accuracy 91.0 %, rare subtype 0 % correct.

**E3.** The "different" labels go to the corners and edges of the pool, far from all earlier labels, including the rare cluster: 4 rare cells are labelled, after which the model learns the corner. Accuracy 95.0 %, rare subtype 81 %.

**E4.** 92.0 % (rare 86 %) with 20 labels; the mean curves at 20: random 85.4 %, uncertain 88.3 %, uncertain + different 92.8 %, mistakes 90.8 %. The catch: someone has to look at the predictions for all cells and recognise the mistakes, which is the human-in-the-loop work; the automatic rules need no person until a cell is proposed.

**E5.** Possible with about 2 labels per region: a few along the middle of each moon's boundary, the ends of both moons, and one or two in the rare cluster. You used both rules at once: uncertainty (near the boundary) and diversity (unexplored regions).
:::

## Code {#code}

Write the algorithms of this unit yourself, in Rust. Setup, and how to run and check your code:
[coding exercises: getting started](../code.qmd). Your code goes in `finetuning/src/few_labels/exercise.rs`.

`finetuning/src/few_labels/model.rs` gives the pool of cells (as in the demo) and the classifier
(`Model::fit(cells, labelled)`, `model.prob(x, y)`, `model.score(test)`).

**C1.** `uncertainty(p)`: $1 - \lvert 2p - 1\rvert$. The check is B3(a).

**C2.** `most_uncertain(probs, labelled)`: the unlabelled cell with the largest uncertainty (ties to the lowest index; `None` if all are labelled). The check is B3.

**C3.** `most_different(cells, labelled)`:

```
best = none
for every unlabelled cell j:
    d = smallest distance from j to a labelled cell
    if d > the best distance so far: best = j
return best
```

The check is B4.

**C4.** `entropy(p)`: $-p\log_2 p - (1 - p)\log_2(1 - p)$, with $0\log 0 = 0$. The check is math question B8's numbers.

Then `cargo run -p finetuning -- few-labels`. The program prints uncertainty and entropy for a
few values, the accuracy with all 500 cells labelled, and the learning curves (mean of 5 starts)
of four rules: random, most uncertain, most different, and both in turn. It saves the pool after
40 labels with each rule in `out/few-labels/`.

**C5.** Compare the uncertainty and the entropy of $p = 0.7$ and $0.9$. Do they rank cells the same way?

**C6.** Which rule is best at 10 labels, and which at 40? Look at the rare-subtype column of "most uncertain", and open `most-uncertain-40.png` and `both-in-turn-40.png`.

**C7.** With all 500 cells labelled the accuracy is 97.3 %. How close does the best rule get with 40?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions (code)"}
The model solution is `finetuning/src/few_labels/solution.rs` in the download.

**C5.** Uncertainty: 1.00, 0.60, 0.20, 0.02 for $p$ = 0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 0.99; entropy: 1.00, 0.88, 0.47, 0.08 bits. Different numbers, the same order (math question B8).

**C6.** At 10 labels: most different 83.5 %, most uncertain 83.3 %, both 82.7 %, random 77.5 %. At 40: both in turn 95.3 %, most different 93.7 %, most uncertain 93.3 %, random 91.9 %. The rare subtype: most uncertain gets 0 % at 10 and 15 labels and 20 % from then on (one of the five starts happens to label a rare cell); both in turn 79 % at 40. In the pictures, most uncertain's labels line the boundary, and the rare corner is coloured as class A; both in turn has labels in the corners too.

**C7.** Both in turn: 95.3 % with 40 labels, 2 points below all 500 (97.3 %), with 8 % of the labels.
:::

## Where this leads

The labels you collect are only valid for the images they came from. The [next unit](../domain-shift/lec.qmd) asks what happens when a model trained on one microscope meets another, and how a few labelled images of the new one help.
